sections.heading: Folk and tribal culture — the people's archive

rows: **Oral epics & ballads**

**Palnati Veerula Katha** (the 'Andhra Kurukshetra' — Brahma Naidu's chapakudu inter-caste feast!), **Katamaraju Katha** (cattle-herders' epic), **Bobbili Katha**, Desingu Raja; **veedhi-bhagavatam** street tellings
Sung by hereditary bards (**pichchukuntla, jangam katha** traditions); epics encode caste-negotiation and heroism — subaltern history in verse
**Performance forms**

**Burrakatha** (3-performer narrative — modernised by praja natya mandali politics), **Harikatha** (Ajjada Adibhatla Narayana Dasu — 'Harikatha pitamaha'), **Tolu bommalata** (leather shadow-puppetry), **Veeranatyam, Butta bommalu, Dappu, Tappeta gullu, Kolatam**, Chindu/Yaksha-ganam of the Madigas
Burrakatha became the freedom movement's loudspeaker (and later the communists'); puppetry carried Ramayana-Mahabharata to the village night
**Tribal cultures (Eastern Ghats agency)**

**Koya, Konda Reddi, Savara (Gidugu's grammar!), Gadaba, Jatapu, Kondh, Valmiki; Chenchus (Nallamala)**; **Dhimsa dance (Araku), Thurpu bhagavatam**; gotti/kolatam variants; shifting-cultivation (podu) lifeworlds; sacred groves & hill deities (Sammakka-Saralamma's cousin-cults)
Culture = economy = rights: podu, NTFP and land alienation are cultural questions too — the fituris (Alluri) defended a lifeworld, not just livelihood
**Subaltern religious culture**

Village goddesses (**grama devatas — Poleramma, Gangamma (Tirupati jatara), Maridamma**), jataras & animal-sacrifice complexes, **Veerabrahmam's Kalagnanam** (the Vishwabrahmin prophet of Kandimallayapalle — egalitarian prophecy tradition; Dudekula Siddayya his Muslim disciple)
Bhakti-from-below: Veerabrahmam's anti-caste prophecy is Andhra's Kabir-parallel — a favourite exam point

sections.heading: Subaltern voices and women's cultural role

items: **Subaltern culture as counter-history**: Madiga Chindu performers, Mala Dasari ritualists, the Jamukula-katha singers preserved caste-critical narrative (the Chennaiah-Jambavanta origin tales asserting Dalit primacy) — 'the defeated keep their own scripture'; modern Dalit assertion (Adi-Andhra 1917) drew on these reservoirs.

**Women as culture-bearers**: the **female oral universe** — lullabies (lali paatalu), grinding-songs, wedding suvvi songs, **Bathukamma's coastal cousins (Gobbemma circles)**, lament traditions; women's tellings of Ramayana (**'Ramayanam of the women's quarters'** — Chandrabati-parallel Telugu variants where Sita's voice leads); vrata-kathas as women's narrative commons; and the professional exceptions — devadasi-court traditions preserving Kshetrayya padams & Kuchipudi's feminine repertoire (with their exploitation-artistry double face, the anti-nautch debate's substance).

**Colonial-modern impact**: census-folklorists collected while missionaries condemned; print marginalised bards; BUT nationalism **re-functionalised** folk forms (burrakatha for swaraj; lambadi/kolatam at Congress meets) and the modern state institutionalised them (Sangeet Natak-style academies, tribal museums — Araku) — the preservation-vs-fossilisation tension is the evaluative close.
**The thesis**: Andhra's identity was built twice — by the literate renaissance (HCOA-056/059/060) and by this **oral commonwealth**; an answer that names both is complete.

blocks.text: Exam tip: The chapakudi (inter-dining) motif of the Palnadu epic and Veerabrahmam's anti-caste Kalagnanam are the two facts that prove folk culture carried social radicalism centuries before the reformers — the connection APPSC loves.

sections.heading: The Justice Party and the non-Brahmin question in Andhra

blocks.text: The **South Indian Liberal Federation ('Justice Party', Madras 1916-17 — T.M. Nair, P. Thyagaraja Chetty, C. Natesa Mudaliar)** answered a real asymmetry: Brahmins (~3% of the Presidency) held the crushing majority of degrees, judgeships and Congress leadership. Its programme — **communal representation in education and services** — produced dyarchy-era ministries (1920-26, 1930-37) and the **Communal G.O.s (1927-era)** rationing posts among communities: **India's first reservation architecture**, the ancestor of today's OBC frame. **Andhra's stake**: leading Justicites were Telugu magnates — the **Raja of Panagal (Panaganti Ramarayaningar, Chief Minister 1921-26**, of Kalahasti's family), **Kurma Venkata Reddy Naidu** (minister; acting Governor's-council rank), koneti/kamma-reddy-velama elite networks; the party's **Andhra wing** fought Brahmin dominance in the new university-bar-secretariat world.

rows: Achievements

**Communal G.O.s** (quota rationing); **Madras University reform; Andhra University's birth (1926) under Panagal's ministry**; temple-administration law (**HRE Act 1926** — state oversight of temples: the HR&CE lineage); Staff Selection-type service boards; women's suffrage resolution (Madras first, 1921)
Institutional social justice — reservations, temple-state relations and AU are its living monuments in AP
Politics & limits

Elite non-Brahminism (zamindar-led, not subaltern); **loyalist tilt** (ministries under dyarchy while Congress boycotted); anti-Brahminism sometimes displacing anti-colonialism; fading after 1937 (Congress sweep), transformed by **Periyar into Dravidar Kazhagam (1944)**
The standard critique: justice for the backward pursued through collaboration with the Raj; yet its quota-grammar outlived its politics
Andhra vs Tamil trajectories

In Tamil country → Dravidian movement & DMK's century; **in Andhra → absorbed into Congress-kisan politics** (kamma-reddy elites moved to Congress/communists by the 1930s); non-Brahminism persisted as social fact, not separate party
Why the difference? Andhra's linguistic-identity politics (Andhra movement) provided the alternative vehicle — a comparison examiners relish

sections.heading: Andhra leaders in the era — the wider gallery

items: **Justice stream**: Panagal Raja (CM 1921-26; the **Panagal-era G.O.s**), Kurma Venkata Reddy Naidu (acting CM 1936 interlude), A. Subbarayalu Reddiar (first Justice CM, 1920 — of Andhra-border lineage), Bollini/Munuswamy-era ministers — plus the **Andhra Non-Brahmin conferences** of the 1920s.

**The Congress counter-gallery** (for balance, same years): Konda Venkatappayya, Prakasam, Pattabhi — Brahmin-led Congress vs Justicite non-Brahminism was Andhra's elite fault line UNTIL kisan radicalism (Ranga) and the Andhra movement rebuilt coalitions across it.

**Legacy audit for AP**: reservations' genealogy (Communal G.O. → post-independence lists → BC quotas), **HR&CE temple governance**, Andhra University, and the normalised presence of non-Brahmin leadership in every later party (NTR's 1980s mobilisation has this pre-history) — Justice's grammar without Justice's loyalism.

sections.heading: The poets' front — nationalist and revolutionary Telugu literature

rows: **Gurram Jashuva (1895-1971)**
***Gabbilam* (1941)** — the Dalit Meghadutam: a bat carries the outcaste's message to Siva; *Firadausi*, *Kandiseekudu*
Dalit suffering made high poetry — 'the poet of the ages' (**Kavi Kokila; Navayuga Kavi Chakravarti**) answering caste with artistry; untouchability's indictment inside the canon
**Boyi Bheemanna (1911-2005)**
***Gudiselu Kalipotunnayi* (huts are burning)**, *Paleru* (the farm-servant play), *Raga Vasistham*
From paleru (bonded farmhand) to Padma Bhushan — literature of Dalit labour; the burning-huts image as the classic of agrarian-caste protest
**Sri Sri (Srirangam Srinivasa Rao, 1910-83)**
***Maha Prasthanam* (written 1930s, pub. 1950)** — 'Mundadugu', 'Desa charitralu'…

The revolution's metronome: '**another world, another world, another world is calling**'; abhyudaya (progressive) poetry's manifesto — Marxist modernism that re-metred Telugu verse; later Viplava Rachayitala Sangham (Virasam, 1970) founding president
**Garimella Satyanarayana (1893-1952)**
**'Maakoddee Tella Dorathanamu' (1921)** — 'we don't want this white lordship'
The Non-Cooperation era's banned anthem — jailed repeatedly for a song; the singing satyagrahi
**Rayaprolu Subbarao (1892-1984)**
*Trunakankanam*, *Andhravali*; **'Edesamegina endukalidina… janani janmabhoomischa'**
Bhava-kavitvam's father AND patriotic lyricist — romantic nationalism's Telugu voice
**Unnava Lakshminarayana (1877-1958)**
***Malapalli* (1922)** — the novel of a Mala village, Gandhian-socialist vision; wrote it in Rayavellore jail; **Sarada Niketanam (women's institution, Guntur)**
The first great social-realist Telugu novel — banned by the Raj; reform + nationalism + Dalit dignity in one canvas
**Tripuraneni Ramaswamy (1887-1943)**
*Sutapuranam*, *Sambhuka Vadha*, *Khooni*; barrister of Tenali — '**Kaviraju**'
Rationalist counter-mythology — rereading Ramayana-puranas from the non-Brahmin standpoint; self-respect weddings' Telugu priest-book (Vivaha Vidhi); the region's Periyar-parallel pen

sections.heading: Reading the front — movements in verse

items: **Three streams, one river**: patriotic-romantic (Rayaprolu, Garimella — and add **Chilakamarthi's 'Bharata Khandambu'** lineage), social-realist reform (Unnava, Jashuva, Bheemanna), and revolutionary-progressive (Sri Sri; the **Abhyudaya Rachayitala Sangham/Arasam (1943)** — with **Praja Natya Mandali** as its stage wing) — Telugu letters marched a half-step ahead of Telugu politics at every turn.

**Literature as organisation**: songs were the movement's logistics — Garimella's anthem at NCM meetings, burrakatha adaptations of Malapalli themes, Sri Sri's metres in the Telangana struggle's squad songs — verse did the work leaflets couldn't (memory + music + mass).

**The caste-question inside the canon**: Jashuva writing INTO the pandit assembly (his avadhanam-circuit triumphs), Bheemanna's paleru autobiography-drama, Tripuraneni's counter-epics — Telugu literature conducted India's caste debate in full public view a generation before national historiography caught up.

**Assessment**: no Indian language shows a tighter weld of poetry and politics in 1920-50; the exam's favourite pairing — **Gabbilam vs Meghadutam** (the messenger inverted: cloud for the exile-lord, bat for the outcaste) — one sentence of it marks literary literacy.
